claim: Selective antagonists of AR and GR did not induce significant modulation of ER dynamics.

evidence: This is a result from the experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: SERMs 4-OHT and GDC-0810 show lower maximal increases in fbound compared with the SERDs fulvestrant and GDC-0927.
source: Interestingly, SERMs 4-OHT and GDC-0810 show lower maximal increases in fbound compared with the SERDs fulvestrant and GDC-0927 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Similar effects to those measured by SMT have been described previously using FRAP.
source: Similar effects have been described previously using FRAP (Guan et al., 2019), which we confirmed using our Halo-ER cell line (Figure 4E).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The delay in ER signal recovery after 2 min in FRAP was consistent with the changes in fbound measured by SMT.
source: The delay in ER signal recovery after 2 min in FRAP was consistent with the changes in fbound measured by SMT (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a comparison between FRAP and SMT results shown in a figure.

claim: Both agonist and antagonist treatment led to longer binding times compared to DMSO.
source: Both agonist and antagonist treatment led to longer binding times compared to DMSO, suggesting that ligand binding decreases k*off (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a result from the residence time experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Ligand binding decreases k*off for ER.
source: Both agonist and antagonist treatment led to longer binding times compared to DMSO, suggesting that ligand binding decreases k*off (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the residence time experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Estradiol, GDC-0927, and fulvestrant show longer binding times compared with other ER modulators.
source: Consistent with FRAP, estradiol, GDC-0927, and fulvestrant show longer binding times compared with other ER modulators.
evidence: This is a result from the residence time experimental data.

claim: In all cases, the changes in dissociation rate are not proportional to the increase in fbound.
source: In all cases, the changes in dissociation rate are not proportional to the increase in fbound, and so ligand-imposed increases in k*on likely contribute to the observed change in the chromatin-associated ER fraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an analysis of the experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Ligand-imposed increases in k*on likely contribute to the observed change in the chromatin-associated ER fraction.
source: In all cases, the changes in dissociation rate are not proportional to the increase in fbound, and so ligand-imposed increases in k*on likely contribute to the observed change in the chromatin-associated ER fraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Compound-induced ER degradation was observed via immunofluorescence in established breast cancer model lines and the U2OS ectopic expression system.
source: We indeed observed compound-induced ER degradation via immunofluorescence, both in established breast cancer model lines and our U2OS ectopic expression system (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a result from the immunofluorescence experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The correlation between ER degradation and cell proliferation is poor for structural analogs of GDC0927.
source: Structural analogs of GDC0927 have been reported and optimized for ER degradation, however the correlation between ER degradation and cell proliferation is poor (Lu and Liu, 2020; Kahraman et al., 2019; Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data shown in figures and supported by citations.

claim: Structural analogues of GDC-0927 exhibited a potency range of 15 pM to 12 nM and increased ER fbound by 0.4–0.56.
source: Overall, these analogues exhibited a potency range of 15 pM to 12 nM and increased ER fbound by 0.4–0.56 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Potency assessed by ER degradation was not a good predictor of potency in the cell proliferation assay.
source: Potency assessed by ER degradation was not a good predictor of potency in the cell proliferation assay (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from comparing different assays shown in a figure.

claim: SMT measurements of fbound strongly correlate with cell viability (R2 of 0.83 for T47d and 0.84 for MCF7).
source: By contrast, SMT measurements of fbound strongly correlate with cell viability (Figure 5C; R2 of 0.83 for T47d and 0.84 for MCF7).
evidence: This is a result from comparing SMT and cell viability assays shown in a figure.

claim: SMT EC50 values were on average tenfold lower than those observed in the cell growth assay.
source: Intriguingly, SMT EC50 values were on average tenfold lower than those observed in the cell growth assay, suggesting that SMT may be sensitive enough to identify chemical series that would not show effects in other cellular assays, enabling the identification of starting points for medicinal chemistry that could not be obtained by other methods.
evidence: This is a result from comparing SMT and cell growth assays.

claim: SMT may be sensitive enough to identify chemical series that would not show effects in other cellular assays.
source: Intriguingly, SMT EC50 values were on average tenfold lower than those observed in the cell growth assay, suggesting that SMT may be sensitive enough to identify chemical series that would not show effects in other cellular assays, enabling the identification of starting points for medicinal chemistry that could not be obtained by other methods.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between SMT and cell growth assays.

claim: 239 compounds in the bioactive library affected the ER mobility using a 5% change in fbound threshold.
source: We found that a 5% change in fbound was sufficient to reproducibly distinguish active compounds. Using this approach, we identified 239 compounds in the bioactive library that affected the ER mobility (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment shown in a figure.

claim: Among active compounds from the bioactive screen, the correlation between the two screen replicates was high (R2 = 0.92).
source: Among these compounds, the correlation between the two screen replicates was high (R2 = 0.92) and the level of activity was reproducible (the slope for active molecules was 0.94).
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment.

claim: The level of activity was reproducible between screen replicates (the slope for active molecules was 0.94).
source: Among these compounds, the correlation between the two screen replicates was high (R2 = 0.92) and the level of activity was reproducible (the slope for active molecules was 0.94).
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment.

claim: Heat shock protein (HSP) inhibitors consistently increased fbound.
source: For example, heat shock protein (HSP) and proteasome inhibitors consistently increased fbound, whereas cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) and mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors decreased fbound.
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment.

claim: Proteasome inhibitors consistently increased fbound.
source: For example, heat shock protein (HSP) and proteasome inhibitors consistently increased fbound, whereas cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) and mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors decreased fbound.
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors decreased fbound.
source: For example, heat shock protein (HSP) and proteasome inhibitors consistently increased fbound, whereas cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) and mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors decreased fbound.
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment.

claim: mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors decreased fbound.
source: For example, heat shock protein (HSP) and proteasome inhibitors consistently increased fbound, whereas cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) and mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors decreased fbound.
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment.

claim: CDK9-specific inhibitors more strongly affected ER dynamics than did CDK4/6-specific inhibitors.
source: Though many CDK inhibitors lack within-family specificity (Wells et al., 2020; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, pan-CDK), we found that CDK9-specific inhibitors more strongly affected ER dynamics than did CDK4/6-specific inhibitors.
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment shown in a figure and supported by citation.

claim: Inhibitors targeting ALK, BTK, and FLT3 kinases have no impact on ER dynamics when assessed using SMT.
source: Furthermore, as with selective AR and GR antagonists, inhibitors targeting ALK, BTK, and FLT3 kinases that have not been shown to interact with ER have no impact on ER dynamics when assessed using SMT (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment shown in a figure.

claim: Potencies of pathway inhibitors ranged from the sub-nanomolar to low micromolar.
source: Potencies ranged from the sub-nanomolar to low micromolar (Figure 6B), similar to the reported potencies of these compounds against their cellular targets (Wang et al., 2018; Olson et al., 2018; Parry et al., 2019; Menezes et al., 2012; McCleese et al., 2009; Bussenius et al., 2012; Apsel et al., 2008; Thoreen et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2009; Adams et al., 1999; Kuhn et al., 2007; Mroczkiewicz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a result from the dose titration experiments shown in a figure and compared to prior work via citations.

claim: The potencies of pathway inhibitors measured by SMT were similar to the reported potencies of these compounds against their cellular targets.
source: Potencies ranged from the sub-nanomolar to low micromolar (Figure 6B), similar to the reported potencies of these compounds against their cellular targets (Wang et al., 2018; Olson et al., 2018; Parry et al., 2019; Menezes et al., 2012; McCleese et al., 2009; Bussenius et al., 2012; Apsel et al., 2008; Thoreen et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2009; Adams et al., 1999; Kuhn et al., 2007; Mroczkiewicz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison between SMT results and prior work supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each SHR differed meaningfully from the others in terms of the response to compounds identified through an ER-focused screening effort.
source: Additionally, we tested these molecules against AR (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) and PR (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D). Each SHR differed meaningfully from the others in terms of the response to compounds identified through an ER-focused screening effort.
evidence: This is a result from testing compounds against multiple SHRs shown in figures.

claim: HSP90 inhibitors increased fbound for ER, AR, and PR.
source: HSP90 is a chaperone for many proteins, including SHRs. In the canonical model, hormone binding releases the SHR–HSP90 complex. Indeed, HSP90 inhibitors increased fbound for ER, AR, and PR, consistent with the hypothesis that one function of the chaperone may be to adjust the equilibrium of SHR binding to chromatin (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is a result from testing HSP90 inhibitors against multiple SHRs shown in figures.

claim: Proteasome inhibition leads to ER immobilization on chromatin.
source: Proteasome inhibition also leads to ER immobilization on chromatin (Stenoien et al., 2001), which aligns with the results that we obtained in our htSMT screen of bioactive compounds.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by the htSMT screen results.

claim: ER has been shown to be phosphorylated by CDK.
source: ER has been shown to be phosphorylated by CDK (Franco et al., 2018), Src (Shah and Rowan, 2005), or GSK-3 through MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling pathways (Anbalagan and Rowan, 2015), and therefore inhibition of these pathways could reasonably be expected to affect ER dynamics measured using SMT.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ER has been shown to be phosphorylated by Src.
source: ER has been shown to be phosphorylated by CDK (Franco et al., 2018), Src (Shah and Rowan, 2005), or GSK-3 through MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling pathways (Anbalagan and Rowan, 2015), and therefore inhibition of these pathways could reasonably be expected to affect ER dynamics measured using SMT.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ER has been shown to be phosphorylated by GSK-3 through MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling pathways.
source: ER has been shown to be phosphorylated by CDK (Franco et al., 2018), Src (Shah and Rowan, 2005), or GSK-3 through MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling pathways (Anbalagan and Rowan, 2015), and therefore inhibition of these pathways could reasonably be expected to affect ER dynamics measured using SMT.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CDK inhibition led to an increase in ER mobility.
source: While CDK inhibition led to an increase in ER mobility, inhibition of PI3K, AKT, or other upstream kinases showed no effect (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment shown in a figure.

claim: Inhibition of PI3K, AKT, or other upstream kinases showed no effect on ER mobility.
source: While CDK inhibition led to an increase in ER mobility, inhibition of PI3K, AKT, or other upstream kinases showed no effect (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment shown in a figure.

claim: SMT dynamics of an ER triple point mutant (S104A/S106A/S118A) were affected by CDK and mTOR pathway inhibitors.
source: Interestingly, SMT dynamics of an ER triple point mutant engineered to lack previously defined phosphorylation sites important for transactivation (Anbalagan and Rowan, 2015) (S104A/S106A/S118A) were affected by CDK and mTOR pathway inhibitors (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggesting that additional phosphorylation sites can mediate the effects of CDK9 and PI3K/AKT signaling, or that other molecular targets of CDK and PI3K/AKT can act indirectly to alter the motion of ER.
evidence: This is a result from testing the ER mutant shown in a figure and supported by citation.

claim: Additional phosphorylation sites can mediate the effects of CDK9 and PI3K/AKT signaling on ER dynamics.
source: Interestingly, SMT dynamics of an ER triple point mutant engineered to lack previously defined phosphorylation sites important for transactivation (Anbalagan and Rowan, 2015) (S104A/S106A/S118A) were affected by CDK and mTOR pathway inhibitors (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggesting that additional phosphorylation sites can mediate the effects of CDK9 and PI3K/AKT signaling, or that other molecular targets of CDK and PI3K/AKT can act indirectly to alter the motion of ER.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ER mutant experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Other molecular targets of CDK and PI3K/AKT can act indirectly to alter the motion of ER.
source: Interestingly, SMT dynamics of an ER triple point mutant engineered to lack previously defined phosphorylation sites important for transactivation (Anbalagan and Rowan, 2015) (S104A/S106A/S118A) were affected by CDK and mTOR pathway inhibitors (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggesting that additional phosphorylation sites can mediate the effects of CDK9 and PI3K/AKT signaling, or that other molecular targets of CDK and PI3K/AKT can act indirectly to alter the motion of ER.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ER mutant experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Both ER agonists and antagonists rapidly induce ER immobilization on chromatin when measured in kSMT (t1/2 = 1.6 min for estradiol).
source: Both ER agonists and antagonists rapidly induce ER immobilization on chromatin when measured in kSMT (t1/2 = 1.6 min for estradiol; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the kinetic SMT experiments shown in a figure.

claim: HSP90 inhibitors like ganetespib and HSP990 exhibit a delay of 5–7 min before alterations in ER dynamics appear.
source: On the other hand, HSP90 inhibitors like ganetespib and HSP990 exhibit a delay of 5–7 min before alterations in ER dynamics appear, after which we observed an increase in fbound with a t1/2 of 19.3 and 17.5 min, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the kinetic SMT experiments.

claim: After the initial delay, HSP90 inhibitors ganetespib and HSP990 showed an increase in fbound with a t1/2 of 19.3 and 17.5 min, respectively.
source: On the other hand, HSP90 inhibitors like ganetespib and HSP990 exhibit a delay of 5–7 min before alterations in ER dynamics appear, after which we observed an increase in fbound with a t1/2 of 19.3 and 17.5 min, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the kinetic SMT experiments.

claim: The overall effect of HSP90 inhibitors reached a plateau after an hour.
source: The overall effect of these compounds reached a plateau after an hour (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from the kinetic SMT experiments shown in a figure.

claim: Proteasome inhibitors bortezomib and carfilzomib acted even more slowly, with changes in ER dynamics emerging only after 40 min.
source: Proteasome inhibitors, for example bortezomib and carfilzomib, acted even more slowly, with changes in ER dynamics emerging only after 40 min, and slowly increasing over the 4-hr measurement window (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the kinetic SMT experiments shown in a figure.

claim: Proteasome inhibitors bortezomib and carfilzomib showed slowly increasing effects over the 4-hr measurement window.
source: Proteasome inhibitors, for example bortezomib and carfilzomib, acted even more slowly, with changes in ER dynamics emerging only after 40 min, and slowly increasing over the 4-hr measurement window (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the kinetic SMT experiments shown in a figure.

claim: Kinetic SMT represents an important tool that can facilitate differentiation between on-target and on-pathway modulators.
source: Hence, this exploration of SMT kinetics represents an important tool that can facilitate differentiation between on-target and on-pathway modulators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic SMT experiments.

claim: HSP90 inhibition by HSP990 and ganetespib resulted in an increase in fbound but a decrease in the total number long binding events by two- and fourfold, respectively.
source: In contrast to the SERDs and SERNs, although HSP90 inhibition by HSP990 and ganetespib resulted in an increase in fbound, we observed a decrease in the total number long binding events by two- and fourfold, respectively, while the binding times were similar to that observed with DMSO alone (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is a result from the residence time experiments shown in figures.

claim: HSP90 inhibition primarily increases k*on while leaving k*off largely unaffected.
source: These results suggest HSP90 inhibition primarily increases k*on while leaving k*off largely unaffected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the residence time experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of the proteasome led to an increase in both the number and duration of long binding events.
source: On the other hand, inhibition of the proteasome led to an increase in both the number and duration of long binding events.
evidence: This is a result from the residence time experiments.

claim: ER–chromatin binding can be modulated by changing the rate of association or disassociation.
source: These results demonstrate that ER–chromatin binding can be modulated by changing the rate of association or disassociation, and that the inhibition of specific cellular partners can affect these rates differentially.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the residence time experimental data.

claim: The inhibition of specific cellular partners can affect ER–chromatin binding rates differentially.
source: These results demonstrate that ER–chromatin binding can be modulated by changing the rate of association or disassociation, and that the inhibition of specific cellular partners can affect these rates differentially.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the residence time experimental data.

claim: Each class of molecule (direct ER modulators, HSP90 inhibitors, proteasome inhibitors) alters ER dynamics through distinct mechanisms.
source: Taken together with the different kinetics for direct ER, HSP90, and proteasome modulators, our data suggest that each class of molecule alters ER dynamics through distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic and residence time experimental data.

claim: The interaction map derived from unbiased htSMT screening recapitulates many known biological interaction partners of the ER.
source: The interaction map derived from unbiased htSMT screening recapitulates many known biological interaction partners of the ER, in a single experimental setup using protein motion as a sole readout.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the screening experimental data.

claim: The impact of HSP inhibition in increasing ER–chromatin association has never been described.
source: To our knowledge, the impact of HSP inhibition in increasing ER–chromatin association has never been described, neither has the link between inhibition post-translation modifying enzymes like the CDKs or mTOR and ER dynamics ever been described.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The link between inhibition post-translation modifying enzymes like the CDKs or mTOR and ER dynamics has never been described.
source: To our knowledge, the impact of HSP inhibition in increasing ER–chromatin association has never been described, neither has the link between inhibition post-translation modifying enzymes like the CDKs or mTOR and ER dynamics ever been described.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: CDK4/6 inhibitors are co-administered with SERDs and SERMs to improve therapeutic outcomes.
source: For example, CDK4/6 inhibitors are co-administered with SERDs and SERMs to improve therapeutic outcomes (Liang et al., 2021; Wardell et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CDK4/6 inhibition only minimally affects ER dynamics in SMT.
source: CDK4/6 inhibition only minimally affects ER dynamics in SMT (Figure 3), supporting the view that the combination of CDK4/6 inhibition with ER antagonists functions through a non-redundant ER-independent mechanism (Finn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a result from the screening experiment shown in a figure.

claim: The combination of CDK4/6 inhibition with ER antagonists functions through a non-redundant ER-independent mechanism.
source: CDK4/6 inhibition only minimally affects ER dynamics in SMT (Figure 3), supporting the view that the combination of CDK4/6 inhibition with ER antagonists functions through a non-redundant ER-independent mechanism (Finn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SMT results supported by citation to prior work.

claim: An increase in fbound provoked by a change in cell conditions suggests that molecular interactions with the protein being analyzed have been stabilized.
source: Mechanistically, an increase in fbound provoked by a change in cell conditions suggests that molecular interactions with the protein being analyzed have been stabilized (either made more probable or longer-lasting), while a decrease in fbound suggests the opposite: molecular interactions that have been made less robust.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of fbound changes.

claim: A decrease in fbound suggests that molecular interactions have been made less robust.
source: Mechanistically, an increase in fbound provoked by a change in cell conditions suggests that molecular interactions with the protein being analyzed have been stabilized (either made more probable or longer-lasting), while a decrease in fbound suggests the opposite: molecular interactions that have been made less robust.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of fbound changes.

claim: ER antagonists may function by promoting ER binding to non-specific decoy chromatin sites.
source: ER antagonists may function by promoting ER binding to non-specific decoy chromatin sites, thus reducing the amount of ER able to activate transcription at ER-responsive genes (Guan et al., 2019; Van Royen et al., 2014; Van Royen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous work has shown that SERDs, and to a lesser extent SERMs, induce an alternate conformation of ER, thereby inhibiting co-factor recruitment.
source: Previous work has also shown that SERDs, and to a lesser extent SERMs, induce an alternate conformation of ER, thereby inhibiting co-factor recruitment (Guan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: If co-factors like CBP and p300 stabilize ER–chromatin binding, then efficacious inhibitors might exhibit shorter binding times compared with agonist stimulation.
source: If co-factors like CBP and p300 stabilize ER–chromatin binding, then efficacious inhibitors might exhibit shorter binding times compared with agonist stimulation (Guan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The SERMs 4-OHT and GDC-0810 dramatically increase ER–chromatin binding frequency and only modestly increase binding times.
source: The SERMs 4-OHT and GDC-0810 dramatically increase ER–chromatin binding frequency and only modestly increase binding times; fulvestrant and GDC-0927 strongly increase both ER–chromatin binding frequency and residence time.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: Fulvestrant and GDC-0927 strongly increase both ER–chromatin binding frequency and residence time.
source: The SERMs 4-OHT and GDC-0810 dramatically increase ER–chromatin binding frequency and only modestly increase binding times; fulvestrant and GDC-0927 strongly increase both ER–chromatin binding frequency and residence time.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: htSMT suggests that agonists and antagonists of SHR signaling operate through a previously unappreciated, unified mechanism of chromatin immobilization.
source: Therefore, htSMT suggests that agonists and antagonists of SHR signaling operate through a previously unappreciated, unified mechanism of chromatin immobilization, meriting further investigation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: SMT measurements proved far more reliable in predicting the ability of an ER antagonist to block cell proliferation than an ER degradation assay.
source: In our hands, these measurements proved far more reliable in predicting the ability of an ER antagonist to block cell proliferation than an ER degradation assay, a conclusion that was only able to be drawn due to the scale of htSMT screening capabilities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different assays.

claim: Saturable dose responses were observed for ER antagonists at much lower concentrations using htSMT than with ER degradation assays.
source: Notably, saturable dose responses were observed for ER antagonists at much lower concentrations using htSMT than with ER degradation assays, suggesting that this method will be more sensitive for identifying novel therapeutic agents than with corresponding traditional assay formats.
evidence: This is a result from comparing htSMT and ER degradation assays.

claim: htSMT will be more sensitive for identifying novel therapeutic agents than corresponding traditional assay formats.
source: Notably, saturable dose responses were observed for ER antagonists at much lower concentrations using htSMT than with ER degradation assays, suggesting that this method will be more sensitive for identifying novel therapeutic agents than with corresponding traditional assay formats.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between htSMT and traditional assays.

claim: SMT can identify promising compounds the activity of which might not otherwise be measurable.
source: Thus, SMT can identify promising compounds the activity of which might not otherwise be measurable, provide insight into their mechanism(s) of action, and in the native environment of the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: SMT can provide insight into compound mechanism(s) of action in the native environment of the cell.
source: Thus, SMT can identify promising compounds the activity of which might not otherwise be measurable, provide insight into their mechanism(s) of action, and in the native environment of the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The application of technologies for measuring protein dynamics at scale will prove broadly applicable to the elucidation of biological mechanisms.
source: In this context, we conclude that the application of technologies for measuring protein dynamics at scale will prove broadly applicable to the elucidation of biological mechanisms.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the broader applicability of the approach.
